planting.note: Tuck small rosette divisions into moss-covered rock crevices or lean gravelly soil in spring; avoid disturbing roots more than necessary.

directions: Nevius' stonecrop is a diminutive, mat-forming succulent native to river-bluff rock outcrops of the southern Appalachians in Tennessee, Alabama, and Georgia, where it roots directly into thin pockets of moss and lichen on gneiss and phyllite ledges. Small rosettes of blue-green, spoon-shaped leaves spread slowly by short stolons, forming loose colonies that hug exposed rock. In late spring, wiry flowering stems lift clusters of small white star-shaped flowers just above the foliage, drawing small native bees and other early-season pollinators. In the garden, give it a sharply drained rock garden, dry-stacked wall, or gravel crevice with light shade and lean soil that mimics its cliffside origins; it resents heavy or consistently moist ground.

planting.note: Divide and plant rosettes in spring into thin, sharply drained soil over rock or a crevice garden gap.

directions: Cliff stonecrop is a rock-outcrop specialist native to the central Appalachians of West Virginia, Maryland, Virginia, and North Carolina, where it clings to shaded sandstone, shale, and limestone ledges with a southern exposure. Rosettes of waxy, glaucous blue-gray leaves form low, spreading colonies that remain evergreen through winter, tinting purplish in cold weather. Clusters of small white flowers open on short stems in late spring, providing nectar for small bees and other pollinating insects before most summer perennials have started blooming. Site plants in a crevice garden, dry stone wall, or thin gravelly soil over rock with light to partial shade, avoiding rich or waterlogged sites where the shallow roots quickly rot.
sources: Digital Atlas of the Virginia Flora

planting.note: Divide established clumps in spring and plant in lean, sharply drained rocky soil; new divisions establish quickly.

directions: Allegheny stonecrop, also called wild live-forever, is an Appalachian native succulent found on rocky outcrops and thin mountain soils from Pennsylvania south to North Carolina, typically at moderate to high elevation. Unlike the low mat-forming stonecrops, it grows as an upright clump of fleshy, blue-green, toothed leaves reaching a foot or more, topped in late summer and early fall by flattened clusters of pale pink to white star-shaped flowers. The late bloom period makes it a valuable native nectar source for bumblebees and other pollinators building up reserves before winter, as well as migrating monarchs passing through the mountains. Grow it in lean, sharply drained, rocky soil in full sun to light shade; established clumps are extremely drought tolerant and need little care beyond occasional dividing to keep them vigorous.
